newsitem.title: MEXICO: U.S. natgas tariff sticking point in Mexican plans.
newsitem.headline: U.S. natgas tariff sticking point in Mexican plans.

text.p: A six percent tariff on Mexican imports of U.S. natural gas is stalling projects and investments in Mexico, as the U.S. government has dragged its feet in removing the tariff, Mexican company and government officials said.

Under the framework of the North American Free Trade Agreement (NAFTA) the natgas tariff is gradually coming down. It was 10 percent when the pact between the United States, Canada and Mexico was signed in 1993 and is scheduled to be completely phased out by 2002.
But now the Mexican government and investors are calling for quicker removal of the tariff, saying it represents a barrier to U.S. natural gas imports.
Imports of the fuel from the United States are important for border communities in northwest Mexico and for a series of multi-million natural gas distribution investments.
"If you want new pipelines and competition for natural gas transportation, you have to take the tariff off," Mexico energy analyst George Baker said.
The six-percent tariff is added to a six-percent transportation cost, for a total 12-percent hike to the price of imported natural gas to Mexico, he added.

Spokesmen for Midcon, a division of Occidental Petroleum Corp, say the additional six-percent charge has stalled construction schedules for a $50 million, 62-km (100 mile) pipeline contract it won from the government in October.
The company has lobbied the U.S. government since February, 1996 to remove the tariff more quickly than scheduled.
But only last week did the United States and Mexico appear to make a definitive step forward.

In Binational Commission meetings earlier this week, Mexico's Energy Minister Jesus Reyes Heroles and U.S. Energy Secretary Federico Pena presented a plan to speed up reduction of the tariff to Mexican Commerce Minister Herminio Blanco.
Blanco said Mexico "is willing to study the proposal," and estimated a decision would be reached by year end.
But for the time being, the tariff is blamed for stalling work on Illinois-based Midcon's project to import natural gas to northern industrial center Monterrey.

Energy Regulatory Commission (CRE) president Hector Olea said Midcon had expected an earlier removal of the tariff, but ran into inaction from the U.S. government and powerful opposition from state oil and gas monopoly Petroleos Mexicanos (Pemex).
"The problem is that the U.S. hasn't asked for it strongly...and Pemex is opposing its removal," Olea said.
Pemex is said to oppose the plan because the Midcon pipeline would compete with natural gas supplied to Monterrey by Pemex.
Recent Mexican privatization laws allow private ownership of new supply pipelines, while existing pipelines must remain in the hands of Pemex.
"With the tariff, Midcon can't compete on a level playing field with Pemex," Olea said.
"Obviously we want to sell at market prices just like Pemex," Midcon spokesman Mike Petitti told Reuters.

He said the company was looking for shipper contracts to buy space on the pipeline to sell natural gas to Mexico. Midcon anticipates building to begin later in the year, with first operations dates still not set, Petitti added.
In addition to the Midcon pipeline, the tariff stands to impede natural gas distribution concessions granted earlier this year.
Denver, Colorado-based KN Energy was granted on Wednesday the rights to distribute natural gas in Hermosillo, Sonora. The fuel would be imported from the United States.
A KN Energy official who declined to be identified said the Mexican consumer will be the victim of a slow tariff removal.
"The tariff is passed through the commodity price, the fuel itself, and will be charged to the customer. It effectively makes the fuel six percent less competitive," he told Reuters.

The Chihuahua state concession, won by a consortium of Enova International, Pacific Enterprises and Mexican company Proxima Gas, could also face the tariff in the future if it switches to U.S. natural gas.
Imported gas is cheaper than Pemex's supply because of regional geography, Olea said.
((--Mexico City newsroom +525 728-7903))
